en: Now begins the first chapter.
Only through the grace of the Lord does the latent impression of non-duality arise in men—those brahmins who are protected from the great fear. (1)
By whom all this is filled—by himself, through himself, within himself—how can I praise that formless, undivided, and imperishable Śiva? 2.
The universe, composed of the five elements, is like water in a mirage;
alas, to whom else should I offer salutations? I alone am the stainless one. (3)
The Self alone is everything; neither difference nor non-difference exists.
How can one speak of "it is" or "it is not"? A sense of wonder appears to me.
The entire essence of the Vedanta is knowledge and realized wisdom itself:
"I am the formless Self, by nature all-pervading. (5)
That very deity who is the self of all, partless, like the sky, pure by nature and stainless—this is he, without a doubt. (6)
I alone am the imperishable, the infinite, whose very form is pure consciousness;
I do not know pleasure or pain—how or for whom could they exist? (7)

I have no mental action, whether auspicious or inauspicious; I have no bodily action, whether auspicious or inauspicious; nor do I have any vocal action, whether auspicious or inauspicious. I am the pure nectar of knowledge, beyond the reach of the senses. (8)
The mind indeed has the form of space; the mind indeed faces in all directions.
The mind transcends the mind; the mind is everything, yet in the ultimate sense, there is no mind.
I see this entire universe as one, beyond the sky and without interval;
how then can I perceive the Self, whether as manifest or as concealed? (10)
Why indeed do you not awaken to this one reality alone, which is impartial toward all and discerned as imperishable?
O Lord, you are ever-risen and undivided; how then can you think [otherwise] by day and by night? 11.
Know yourself to be eternally one and continuous everywhere;
"I am the meditator, and the Supreme is the object of meditation"—how can that which is indivisible ever be divided? (12)
You are neither born nor dead, nor does a body ever belong to you;
"All is Brahman"—thus the Veda proclaims in many ways. 13.
You are Śiva, both internal and external, everywhere and at all times;
why then do you wander here and there, running about like a ghost? 14.
Union and separation occur, yet they belong neither to you nor to me;
neither you, nor I, nor this world exists—everything is solely the Self alone. 15.
You are not this pentad of sound and the other sense-objects, nor do they belong to you;
you alone are the supreme reality—so why do you grieve? 16.
Birth and death do not exist for you; neither bondage nor liberation, nor the auspicious and inauspicious, belong to you.
Why do you weep, O child? Neither name nor form belongs to you, nor to me.
"O mind, how have you wandered so deluded that you run about like a demon?
Behold yourself as undivided; become happy through the abandonment of passion. (18)

You alone are indeed the reality, free from modification, unwavering, one, and the very embodiment of liberation. You possess neither passion nor dispassion; why then do you suffer from the longing for desires? (19)
All the Vedas declare that reality to be devoid of qualities, pure, immutable, bodiless, and equal; know Me to be that, without a doubt. (20)
Know that which has form to be false, and that which is formless to be continuous;
through this instruction on reality, there is no further occurrence of rebirth. (21)
For the wise declare that reality is indeed one and the same;
through the abandonment of passion, the mind is neither one nor many. 22.
How can that which is non-self be the nature of samādhi, and how can samādhi be the nature of the self?
How can samādhi be "it exists" or "it does not exist," if everything is of one single nature, which is the very essence of liberation? (23)
"You are pure, you are the equal reality, bodiless, unborn, and undecaying.
How can you consider yourself, thinking, 'I know here' or 'I do not know'? (24)
For one's own Self is indeed established by such statements as "That thou art";
the Śruti, saying "not this, not this," would then be declaring the five-elemental [body] to be unreal. (25)

Everything is entirely and continuously filled by you within yourself through yourself; there is neither meditator nor meditation, nor even a mind—how then can that which is devoid of shame meditate? 26.
I do not know Śiva; how can I speak of Śiva? I do not know Śiva; how can I worship Śiva?
If I am Śiva, then the reality of the ultimate truth is of a uniform nature and like the sky. ||27||
How could I [know] reality—that equal reality which is free from the causes of conceptual construction, devoid of the grasped and the grasper, and which is to be personally realized? (28)
There is no entity whatsoever that possesses a manifold form, nor is there any entity whatsoever that possesses the nature of ultimate reality;
the supreme truth of reality has the single form of the Self—there is neither the doer of violence nor even non-violence. (29)
You are pure, the equal reality, bodiless, unborn, and immutable;
how then have you fallen into delusion regarding your own self, and how was I so utterly bewildered? 30.
When the jar is broken, the space within the jar is well-absorbed and devoid of division;
purified by my mind through Śiva, no distinction appears to me. 31.
There is neither the pot, nor the space within the pot, nor the individual soul (jīva), nor the body of the individual soul;
know that there is only Brahman alone, devoid of both the object of knowledge and the knower. 32.
Know me, without any doubt, as that which is everywhere, at all times, everything, the self, eternal, and constant; which is both entirely empty and not empty. 33.
Neither the Vedas, nor the worlds, nor the gods, nor sacrifices; neither the system of castes and stages of life, nor family, nor birth;
neither the path of smoke nor the path of light—the ultimate reality is Brahman alone, whose form is one. (34)
If you alone, being free from both the pervaded and the pervader, possess fruitfulness, then how can you consider yourself as both perceptible and immediately apparent? 35.
Some desire non-duality, while others desire duality;
they do not find the reality that is equal and free from both duality and non-duality.
How can they describe that reality which is devoid of colors such as white and the like, which is free from qualities such as sound, and which is beyond the reach of mind and speech? (37)
When all this is unreal, like the body and so forth which are comparable to the sky, then indeed one realizes Brahman; for you, there is no succession of duality.
For even my own innate self appears to me as non-different from another;
likewise, since space is one and of such a form, how can there be a meditator and meditation? (39)
Whatever I do, whatever I eat, whatever I offer in sacrifice, and whatever I give—all this is nothing to me; I am pure, unborn, and immutable.
Know this entire world to be formless; know this entire world to be devoid of transformation;
know this entire world to be a pure body; know this entire world to be of the singular nature of Śiva. ||41||
"You are indeed that reality, there is no doubt; or rather, what do you know?
How can you consider yourself the Self, which is unperceivable yet self-perceived? (42)
O Father, how can there be illusion or non-illusion, or shadow or non-shadow?
All this is a single reality, having the form of space and free from taint. 43.
I am free from beginning, middle, and end; I am never bound.
My mind is certain that I am pure and naturally stainless. 44.
The entire world, beginning with the Mahat, does not appear as anything at all to me;
Brahman alone is everything—how then can there be the established order of castes and stages of life? 45.
I alone know everything in every way and without interruption; I know the five elements, such as space and the rest, which are without support, non-empty, yet empty. 46.
Neither neuter, nor male, nor female; neither consciousness nor even conceptual construction.
How can you conceive of the Self as either with bliss or without bliss? (47)
It is not purified by the six-limbed yoga, nor indeed is it purified by the dissolution of the mind;
it is not purified by the teacher’s instruction, nor indeed is it purified otherwise; for the reality itself is realized by oneself alone. 48.
For the body, consisting of the five elements, does not exist as something bodiless;
indeed, the Self alone is everything—how then could there be a fourth state distinct from the three? 49.
I am neither bound nor am I liberated; I am not distinct from Brahman.
I am neither an agent nor an enjoyer, being devoid of both the pervaded and the pervader. 50.
Just as water poured into water is water devoid of distinction, so too does Prakṛti appear to me as non-different from Puruṣa. 51.
Even if you are indeed neither liberated nor bound at any time, how can you conceive of the Self as both having form and being formless? (52)
I know your supreme form directly, which is like the sky;
for that supreme form is indeed like water in a mirage. 53.
There is no guru for me, nor instruction, nor limiting adjunct, nor ritual action;
know me to be bodiless like the sky, pure by my very nature. (54)
"You are pure in body, yet your mind is not the supreme beyond the supreme;
you do not feel shame to say, 'I am the Self, the ultimate reality. (55)
Why do you weep, O mind? Indeed, let the self alone become the self by itself.
Drink, my child, the supreme nectar of non-duality that transcends all parts. 56.
Neither awakening, nor non-awakening, nor even that which is both awakening and non-awakening—for one whose awareness is always of such a nature, that is true awakening; it cannot be otherwise. (57)
Knowledge is neither logic nor meditative absorption, neither place nor time, nor the instruction of a guru;
it is the self-awareness of my own nature—the reality that is like space, innate, and eternal. 58.
I am neither born nor dead, nor do I possess auspicious or inauspicious karma;
I am the pure, quality-less Brahman—O friend, how can there be bondage or liberation for me? 59.
If the Lord is omnipresent, stable, complete, and without interval, then since I perceive no interval whatsoever, how can he be both external and internal? (60)
The entire universe vibrates indeed as an undivided and continuous whole; oh, what great delusion is this "great Māyā," which consists of the conceptualization of duality and non-duality! 61.
With form and without form, as "not this, not this" at all times—
Śiva alone exists, forever free from both difference and non-difference.
Neither mother nor father, nor kinsman; neither wife nor son, nor friend;
neither partial to one's own side nor hostile to another—how then can there be such torment in the heart? (63)
Day and night your mind has neither rising nor setting;
how can the wise conceive of you, who are bodiless, as having a body? (64)
Know that the Self is imperishable—neither undivided nor divided, neither sorrow nor happiness, and neither the whole nor the part. 65.
I am neither the doer nor the enjoyer, and I have no karma in the past or now;
I have neither a body nor a bodiless state, for I am free from "mine-ness"—so what is there to be called "mine"?
I have no defects such as passion and the like; I have no suffering such as the body and so forth.
Know me to be the one Self alone, vast and comparable to the sky. (67)
O friend, O mind, what is the use of much prattling? O friend, O mind, all this must be reflected upon.
That which is the essence has been told by me to you; you yourself are the reality, like the sky. (68)
By whatever state of being they may die, wherever it may be, yogins dissolve there like the space within a jar merging into the infinite sky. 69.
Whether at a sacred ford or in the house of an outcaste, even one who loses consciousness while casting off the body shall,
at that very moment, become liberated and pervade the state of absolute isolation (kaivalya).
Yogins regard everything—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as all moving and stationary beings from the two-footed onwards—as being like water in a mirage. (71)
"Regarding past and future karma, and likewise the present, my mind is firm in this resolve: 'I do not perform it, nor do I experience its fruit. (72)
Staying alone in an empty house, purified by the flavor of equanimity, the Avadhūta dwells in happiness;
indeed, wandering naked and having abandoned pride, he finds everything within the Absolute Self. 73.
There is no triad, nor even a fourth; where one finds only the Absolute Self, there is neither merit nor demerit.
Where there is neither bondage nor liberation, how can there be such things here? 74.
He finds it, he finds it—not a mantra, not the characteristics of meter, not a tantra;
immersed in the flavor of equanimity (samarasa) and purified through meditation, this supreme Avadhūta utters these words as mere chatter. ||75||
Neither total emptiness nor non-emptiness, neither truth nor untruth exists;
this is declared according to the intrinsic nature of things, preceded by the realization of the scriptures. (76)
Thus ends the first chapter. ||1||
Now begins the second chapter.

Whether he be a child, one addicted to the enjoyment of sense-objects, a fool, or a servant living at home—none of these should ever consider this [teaching] of the Guru. How could anyone discard a jewel that has entered into something impure? ||1||
In this matter, however, it is not the poetic quality alone that should be considered or accepted; rather, it is indeed the essential substance that belongs to one possessed of qualities.
Does a boat on this earth, though devoid of decorative vermilion and lacking beauty, fail to carry those desiring to reach the further shore? (2)
By that which is motionless and free from effort, the ever-shifting world is naturally swallowed up; it is consciousness, tranquil and like the sky. ||3||
If one could move even a single thing among the moving and the unmoving without effort, how could that which is all-pervading be divided? For me, it exists as non-dual. 4.
For I alone am the supreme Śiva, the essence of essences,
free from coming and going, beyond conceptual construction, and undisturbed.
Just as I am free from all constituent parts, so too, though worshipped by the thirty gods,
I do not accept any portion from the gods and others because of my perfection.
Through negligence there is no doubt as to what I shall do while maintaining my livelihood;
beings arise and dissolve just like bubbles in water. (7)
For in this way, the elements beginning with Mahat always pervade soft substances, as well as sharp ones, sweets, and pungent things. (8)
Just as pungency, coolness, and softness exist in water,
so too do Prakṛti and Puruṣa appear to me as inseparable.
That which is devoid of all designations, subtler than the subtlest, supreme, beyond mind, intellect, and the senses, stainless—the Lord of the World. (10)
Where such an innate [nature] exists, how could "I" exist there?
Indeed, how could you yourself exist there, and how could the world of moving and non-moving beings exist there? 11.
That which is said to be like the sky is indeed like the sky:
consciousness, free from defects, omniscient, and truly full. ||12||
It does not move upon the earth, nor is it carried away by the wind; it is not covered by water, nor does it abide within the midst of fire. (13)
By him the sky is pervaded, yet it is not pervaded by anything;
he abides both outside and inside, undivided and without interval. 14.

Because of its subtlety, its invisibility, and its being devoid of qualities, that which has been described by yogis as the object of focus and so forth becomes, in due order, the focal support (ālambana). ||15||
But when one who is engaged in constant practice becomes supportless, through absorption in that [state], he dissolves away, freed from both internal qualities and defects. 16.
For the destruction of this world-poison—which is fierce and brings about the fainting of delusion—there is indeed only one unfailing remedy: innate nectar. (17)
Accessible through meditative cultivation, formless yet appearing with form, within the range of vision, and liberated from both existence and non-existence—that is called the intermediate state. 18.
The universe exists as the external state, while that which is within is called Prakṛti;
one should know that which is more internal than the internal, like the water inside a coconut fruit. 19.
Erroneous cognition is situated on the outside, while correct cognition is in the middle;
that which is more central than the middle should be known as being like the water inside a coconut fruit. 20.
Just as on the full moon night the moon alone is exceedingly pure, one should perceive that which is similar to it; to see it as dual is a perversion.
In this very manner, the diversity of intellects is not all-pervasive;
and the giver attains steadfastness and is celebrated by millions of names. ||22||
Whether one is a fool or a scholar, through the grace of the guru’s wisdom, he who realizes the truth becomes dispassionate toward the ocean of worldly existence. (23)
Freed from passion and hatred, devoted to the welfare of all beings, firm in awakening and steadfast, he shall go to the supreme state. 24.
Just as when a jar is broken, the space within the jar merges into the [great] space, so too, in the absence of the body, the yogi merges into his own true nature, the Supreme Self. 25.
This destination which has been described is for those whose minds are intent on action;
it is not the destination described for those whose minds are disciplined in yoga, even at the time of their departure. ||26||

The destination attained by those engaged in ritual action is that which one speaks through the organ of speech; however, the destination of yogis, which is everywhere unutterable, is attained through their own power. 27.
Having thus understood this path, which is not at all imagined by yogins, their own accomplishment proceeds through the abandonment of conceptual construction. 28.
Whether he dies at a sacred ford, in the house of an outcaste, or wherever else, the yogin does not enter a womb; he dissolves into the supreme Brahman. 29.
He who perceives the innate, unborn, and inconceivable nature of the self may act as he pleases; he is never stained by faults.
Even if that [realization] occurs but once, one would not perform any further action; nor is he bound, whether he be a self-restrained ascetic or a practitioner of austerity. (30)
One attains that eternal Lord, the Self, who is free from disease, peerless, formless, independent, bodiless, desireless, beyond dualities, devoid of delusion, and whose power is never lost. (31)
Where neither Veda, nor initiation, nor the rite of tonsure exists; where there is no guru, no disciple, nor the perfection of yantras;
and where even mudrās and the like do not appear—there one attains that eternal Lord, who is the Self. (32)

Neither the Śāmbhava, Śākta, nor Āṇava [means], nor the Piṇḍa, Rūpa, Padādi, and so forth, nor the jar and other objects produced through the process of commencement—none of these reach that eternal Lord who is the Self. ||33||

From whose own nature the entire world, with its moving and unmoving beings, arises, persists, and even dissolves—just as foam and bubbles from a modification of water—one attains that eternal Lord, the Self. (34)
Where neither the cessation of the breath nor the gaze, nor sitting, nor even awakening or non-awakening shines forth;
where there is not even the movement of the channels—there one attains that eternal Lord, the Self. 35.

Free from multiplicity, unity, duality, otherness, minuteness, length, greatness, emptiness, the state of being a means of knowledge, the state of being an object of knowledge, and even equality—one attains that eternal Lord, the Self. ||36||
Whether he is well-restrained or not restrained, whether he is a good gatherer or not a gatherer, whether he is free from action or possessed of action—he attains that eternal Lord, the Self. ||37||

Neither mind, nor intellect, nor body, nor sense organ, nor the subtle elements, nor the five gross elements, nor even the ego—He who has the nature of space approaches that eternal Lord, the Self. 38.

When the mind of the yogi—devoid of all differentiation—has entered the state of supreme selfhood through the cessation of mental activity, there is neither purity nor impurity; for when the perception of signs has vanished, everything may be either enjoined or prohibited. (39)
Where neither mind nor speech is able to express it, how indeed can there be instruction from a guru?
Yet, when a teacher has spoken this discourse, the reality corresponding to it shines forth equally for one who is devoted to it.
Thus ends the second chapter. ||2||
Now begins the third chapter.

There exists no distinction whatsoever between quality and defect; it is stainless, free from conceptual proliferation, devoid of pleasure and pain, and bereft of both virtue and vice. How can I here not bow to that Śiva, who is all-pervading, whose form is the universe, and whose nature is like the sky? 1.
Devoid of colors such as white and the like, Śiva is certainly the cause, for this effect is indeed the supreme Śiva;
thus, being free from conceptual construction, I am fully Śiva—O good friend, how can I bow to my own Self within myself? ||2||

For I am eternally risen, devoid of roots and even the rootlessness; for I am eternally risen, devoid of smoke and even the absence of smoke; for I am eternally risen, devoid of lamps and even the absence of lamps; I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. ||3||
How can I speak here of "desire for the desireless," or how can I speak here of "attachment to the unattached"?
And how can I speak of the nectar of knowledge as being devoid of essence and substance? I am the equal flavor, like the sky. ||4||
How can I speak of the entire world as non-dual, and how can I speak of the entire world as dual?
How can I speak of the eternal as transient? I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, comparable to the sky. (5)
I am indeed neither gross nor subtle, neither coming nor going, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and neither high nor low.
Truly I speak the ultimate reality; I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. (6)
Realize that all the organs of perception are like the sky; realize that all objects of experience are also like the sky.
Realize the one stainless Self, which is neither bound nor liberated—the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, and like the ether: "I am such. (7)
O Father, I am not a dense thicket for those who find it difficult to understand; O Father, I am not a dense thicket for those whose perception is hard to fix.
O Father, I am not a dense thicket for those who are near [to me]; I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, and like the sky. (8)
I am the blazing fire that consumes the fuel of karma; I am the blazing fire that consumes the suffering of suffering;
I am the blazing fire that consumes the body within the body. I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. 9.
I am indeed the sacrificial fire that burns away both sin and merit; I am indeed the sacrificial fire that burns away both unrighteousness and righteousness;
I am indeed the sacrificial fire that burns away attachment and bondage; I am the nectar of knowledge, equal in flavor, and like the sky. ||10||
O child, I am not devoid of being yet free from existence; O child, I am not devoid of yoga yet free from practice;
O child, I am not devoid of mind yet free from thought; I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. (11)
"I am beyond the state of delusion and non-delusion"—this is not my conceptualization; "I am beyond the state of sorrow and non-sorrow"—this is not my conceptualization;
"I am beyond the state of greed and non-greed"—this is not my conceptualization. I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. 12.
The creeper of the stream of saṃsāra has never existed for me, nor has there ever been for me the happiness of the stream of contentment;
this bondage of ignorance has never existed for me, nor has there ever been for me the nectar of knowledge; I am of equal flavor [with all], like the sky. ||13||
The dust of the continuity of saṃsāra is not a modification for me; the darkness of the continuity of affliction is not a modification for me.
The essence that generates one's own dharma is not a modification for me; I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. (14)
The ritual procedure never produces the suffering of affliction, nor does the mind ever produce that which is born from the conjunction of affliction;
for this ego-sense is never mine, as I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, and like the sky. 15.

I am the nectar of knowledge, equal in flavor and like the sky; I am the cessation of both the unmoving and the moving, yet not the destruction of the moving and the unmoving; I am the cessation of both the beneficial and the harmful, yet not the destruction of the beneficial and the harmful; I am the cessation of both the unreal and the real, yet not the destruction of the unreal and the real; I am the cessation of both the non-conceptual and the conceptual, yet not the destruction of the non-conceptual and the conceptual; I am the cessation of both sleep and waking, yet not the destruction of sleep and waking. (16)
This is neither the object of knowledge nor the knower, nor is it to be inferred through causes; it is beyond the reach of words, neither mind nor intellect.
How then can I describe this reality to you? I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. (17)
The ultimate reality is devoid of both the undifferentiated and the differentiated; it exists neither internally nor externally—how then could it not be the ultimate reality?
It has no prior origin, nor is it an object of attachment; it is not any [ordinary] entity at all. I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. 18.
I alone am that reality which is free from defects such as passion; I alone am that reality which is free from defects such as fate;
I alone am that reality which is free from the sorrows of saṃsāra; I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. (19)
If the three states do not exist, how can there be a fourth? If the three times do not exist, how can there be the directions?
For I am the peaceful state, the supreme reality of the ultimate truth, the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, and like the sky. //20//
"Long" or "short"—I have no such distinction here; "broad" or "narrow"—I have no such distinction here;
"angular" or "circular"—I have no such distinction here. I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. 21.
Mother, father, and so forth, as well as sons and the like, have never been born for me, nor have they ever died; my mind has never been otherwise.
This supreme reality is undisturbed and steadfast—the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor; I am like the sky. 22.

I am pure, utterly purified, beyond thought, and of infinite form; untainted, yet appearing as if tainted, beyond thought, and of infinite form; partless, yet appearing as if divided, beyond thought, and of infinite form; the nectar of knowledge, of uniform essence, I am like the sky. 23.
How can the hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, exist here? How can abodes such as heaven exist here?
If I am the one, stainless, ultimate reality—the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, and like the sky—[then how can these things exist]? ||24||
How can I describe that which is beyond "this" and "not this," for it is stainless? How can I describe that which is stainless, having transcended all that remains?
How can I describe that which is stainless, being devoid of all marks? I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. 25.
I constantly perform that supreme action which is beyond all action; I am the supreme diversion, free from attachment and devoid of worldly bonds.
I am the eternal delight, bodiless and transcending the physical body; I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, and like the sky. 26.
The construction of the manifold play of illusion is not a modification of me; the construction of crookedness and deceit is not a modification of me;
the construction of truth and falsehood is not a modification of me. I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. 27.
I am devoid of the times of twilight and the like, yet not separated from internal awakening; I am neither deaf nor mute.
Thus, free from conceptual construction and pure of all states of being, I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, and like the sky. 28.
Indeed, it is devoid of a lord and free from a master; indeed, it is untroubled and free from the mind and mental objects;
indeed, it is untroubled and free from all consciousness. I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. 29.
How can I say that this is a forest or a house? How can I say that this is a state of doubt or a state of perfection?
Indeed, I am like the sky—the nectar of knowledge, uniform, undisturbed, and of equal flavor. 30.
Devoid of both the soul and the life-force, it shines eternally; devoid of both seed and the state of being seedless, it shines eternally;
devoid of both liberation and bondage, it shines eternally—I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. 31.
This always shines forth devoid of origination; this always shines forth devoid of saṃsāra;
this always shines forth devoid of dissolution. I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. (32)
There is not even a mere mention of name and form for you, nor is there any distinct entity whatsoever;
O shameless-minded one, why do you feel despondency? I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. (33)
Why indeed do you weep, my friend? There is neither old age nor death; why indeed do you weep, my friend? Nor is there the suffering of birth.
Why indeed do you weep, my friend? Nor is there any transformation for you; I am the nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. (34)
Why indeed do you weep, O friend? Your form is not what it seems; why indeed do you weep, O friend? You are not deformed.
Why indeed do you weep, O friend? You are not subject to the stages of life. I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. ||35||
Why do you weep, O friend? Your vital breaths have not departed; why do you weep, O friend? Your minds have not perished.
Why do you weep, O friend? Your senses have not failed. I am the immortal nectar of knowledge, of uniform flavor, like the sky. ||36||
Why do you weep, my friend? You have no desire; why do you weep, my friend? You have no longing.
Why do you weep, my friend? You have no delusion; I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. (37)

You desire sovereignty, yet you have no wealth; you desire sovereignty, yet you have no wife. You desire sovereignty, yet you do not have "mine"—I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. (38)
The birth of the manifold world of gender signs belongs neither to you nor to me; this shameless mind appears as something distinct.
Yet the nectar of knowledge, which is without distinction or duality, belongs neither to you nor to me; I am of a single flavor, like the sky. 39.
Not even an atom of them has the form of dispassion, nor indeed an atom of them has the form of passion;
not even an atom of them has the form of desire. I am the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, like the sky. 40.
There is no meditator in your heart, nor is there concentration or meditation in your heart, nor is there any external location;
there is no object of meditation in the heart, nor indeed any substance, time, or the nectar of knowledge—equal in flavor, I am like the sky. 41.
All that has been told by me to you as the very essence is neither you, nor I, nor the Great One, nor the Guru, nor the disciple;
it is the ultimate reality, whose nature is innate and spontaneous, the nectar of knowledge, of equal flavor, and I am like the sky. 42.
How is it that here the ultimate reality is of the nature of bliss? How is it that here the ultimate reality is not of the nature of bliss?
How is it that here the ultimate reality is of the nature of knowledge and discernment, if indeed I alone exist as the supreme, whose form is space? 43.
Know that consciousness alone is devoid of fire and wind; know that the form of consciousness is devoid of earth and water.
Know that consciousness alone is devoid of the coming together [of elements]; know that consciousness alone is as vast as the sky. 44.
I am neither the form of emptiness nor the form of non-emptiness; neither the form of purity nor the form of impurity.
I do not become any form whatsoever—whether beautiful or ugly—for the ultimate reality is the nature of my own true self. 45.
Abandon, abandon indeed this saṃsāra; abandon renunciation in every way.
Pure, nectar-like, innate, and eternal is that which is free from the poison of both renunciation and non-renunciation. 46.
Thus ends the third chapter. ||3||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
There is neither invocation nor dismissal; how do flowers and leaves come to be? How do meditations and mantras come to be, as well as the worship of Śiva, both equal and unequal? ||1||
I am not merely liberated from bondage and its absence, nor merely liberated through pure purification;
I am not merely liberated from union and separation—I am indeed the liberated one, like the sky. ||2||
All this indeed arises as real; all this arises as unreal.
Such a conceptual construction has never arisen in me; I am the Nirvana of my own true nature, free from ailment.

Neither with attributes nor without attributes, neither with interval nor without interval—indeed, no internal differentiation shines forth for me; I am the blissful extinction of my own nature, free from all ailment.
Neither the awakening of ignorance nor awakening itself has ever arisen for me; the very nature of awakening has never arisen for me.
How can I speak of an awakening devoid of ignorance? I am the self-nature of liberation, free from all affliction. ||5||
I am neither joined with dharma nor joined with sin; I am neither joined with bondage nor joined with liberation.
Neither the "joined" nor the "unjoined" appears to me, for I am the Nirvana of my own true nature, free from all ailment.
Neither superior nor inferior have I ever been, nor indeed have I the state of being neutral, nor am I an enemy or a friend.
How could I speak of benefit or harm? I am the very nature of nirvāṇa, free from all ailment. (7)
I am neither a devotee, nor is there such a form to be worshipped, nor is there instruction, nor is there any ritual action for me.
How can I speak of the nature of consciousness? I am the self-natured Nirvana, free from all ailment.
Here there is nothing that is either the pervader or the pervaded, nor is there anything with a foundation or without a foundation;
how can I speak of non-emptiness and emptiness? I am the Nirvana of my own true nature, free from all affliction. //9//
There is no grasper, nor indeed any object to be grasped; for me there is neither cause nor effect.
How can I speak of that which is both inconceivable and beyond thought? I am the very nature of nirvana, free from all affliction. 10.
There is for me neither the divider nor the divided, neither the knower nor the known;
O dear one, how can I speak of coming and going? I am the nirvana of my own true nature, free from all affliction. (11)
There is no body for me, nor is there for me the notion of being bodiless; I have neither mind nor senses.
How can I speak of passion or dispassion? I am the self-nature of nirvana, free from all ailment.
The mere appearance is not at all distinct, nor indeed is the mere appearance concealed;
O friend, how can I speak of it as equal or unequal? I am the blissful extinction of my own nature, free from all ailment. 13.
Whether I am one who has conquered the senses or one whose senses are unconquered, neither self-restraint nor discipline has arisen in me.
O friend, how can I speak of victory or defeat? I am the very nature of nirvana, free from all ailment. ||14||
I am neither formless nor possessed of form, and never have I beginning, end, or middle;
O friend, how can I speak of strength or weakness? I am the self-nature of nirvana, free from all affliction.
O dear one, for me death never becomes immortality, nor does poison ever become non-poison;
how then can I speak of impurity or purity? I am the self-natured nirvāṇa, free from all ailment. (16)
There is neither sleep nor waking, nor the yoga-mudrā for me, neither by night nor by day at any time.
How can I speak of that which is beyond the fourth state? I am the Nirvāṇa of my own true nature, free from all ailment. ||17||

Know me to be liberated from all and everything; illusion (māyā) and the absence of illusion (vimāyā) never exist for me. How can I speak of rituals such as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), when I am the Nirvāṇa of my own true nature, free from ailment? ||18||
Know me as endowed with all meditative absorptions; know me as liberated from both the object of perception and the act of perceiving.
How can I speak of union or separation? I am the nirvāṇa of my own true nature, free from all affliction.
I am neither a fool nor a scholar; for me there is never silence nor the breaking of silence.
How could I speak of reasoning or counter-reasoning? I am the blissful extinction of my own nature, free from all ailment. (20)
Neither father nor mother, nor family, nor birth, nor death ever belong to me;
how then could I speak of affection or delusion? I am the self-natured nirvana, free from all ailment.
I have never set, nor am I ever risen; there is neither light nor darkness for me at any time.
How can I speak of rituals such as the twilight prayers? I am the Nirvana of my own true nature, free from all affliction.
Know me without doubt to be undisturbed; know me without doubt to be uninterrupted;
know me without doubt to be stainless—I am the Nirvana of my own nature, free from ailment. 23.
They abandon all meditative absorptions and they abandon both auspicious and inauspicious karma;
O dear one, the wise drink the nectar of renunciation—I am the stainless Nirvana of my own true nature.
He finds, he finds—indeed, indeed, where there is no characteristic of desire; indeed, indeed, not there.
Immersed in the flavor of equanimity, purified through meditation, the supreme ascetic utters the truth. 25.
Thus ends the fourth chapter. ||4||
Now begins the fifth chapter.

"Oṃ"—thus it is spoken, equal to the sky, for there is no investigation into the essence of the higher or the lower. How can there be the utterance of syllables and points when all display and non-display have been eliminated? (1)
Thus, through such scriptural texts as "That thou art," it has been established that you are the Reality within the Self.
You are devoid of limiting adjuncts and equal to all; why then do you weep? Be equanimous toward all. 2.
That which is entirely equal, devoid of above and below; entirely equal, devoid of outside and inside;
and if it is entirely equal, devoid of even oneness—then why do you weep, O mind, which is itself entirely equal? (3)

For there is no investigation of the imagined and the imagination, nor indeed any investigation of cause and effect. Free from the junctions of words, all is equal; O mind, why do you weep? All is equal. 4.
For there is no such thing as a samādhi of awakening or non-awakening; for there is no such thing as a samādhi of this place or another place;
for there is no such thing as a samādhi of this time or another time. Why then do you weep, O mind, when all is equal?
For the pot is not different from the space within it, nor is the pot [itself] non-existent; the body is not different from the living soul, nor is the living soul non-existent;
there is no real division between cause and effect—why then do you weep, O mind, when everything is equal?
In this state, the ground of universal liberation is devoid of short or long deliberations;
for there is no distinction between roundness and corners—O mind, why do you weep, when everything is equal? (7)
"Here, one is devoid of emptiness and non-emptiness; here, one is devoid of purity and impurity;
here, one is devoid of everything and nothing—why then do you weep, O Mānasī, who are equal toward all? (8)

For there is no investigation into "different" or "not different," nor an investigation into the junction between the internal and external. O mind, why do you weep? Everything is equal, being devoid of enemy and friend; everything is equal. (9)
For there is no distinction between the nature of the disciple and the teacher, nor is there any consideration of the difference between the moving and the unmoving.
Here, the state of liberation is entirely uninterrupted; why then do you weep, O mind, when everything is equal? 10.

Surely you are devoid of beauty and deformity; surely you are devoid of difference and non-difference; surely you are devoid of creation and dissolution—why then do you weep, O mind, which is equal toward all? 11.
"I am not bound by the fetters of merit and demerit; how then can I perform the act of reviving the dead?
Thus, O mind, why do you weep for that which is pure, stainless, and equal to all—indeed, equal to everything? 12.
"Here, it is devoid of both existence and non-existence; here, it is devoid of both desire and its cessation.
Here, indeed, is the supreme awakening, equal to liberation; why then do you weep, O mind, for that which is equal to all? (13)
In this state, reality is uninterrupted reality; for it is indeed devoid of both connection and disconnection.
If it is entirely free from all distinctions and equal to all, why then do you weep, O mind? It is equal to everything. 14.

O mind, why do you weep—though you are like a hut without a dwelling, devoid of attachment to this world, supreme in its freedom from bonds, and utterly beyond the awakening of worldly consciousness, being equal toward all? 15.
That which is unchanging is unreal, and that which is changing is unreal; that which is undifferentiated is unreal, and that which is differentiated is unreal.
If the Self alone is real, why do you weep, O mind? It is the same for all.
In this world, the soul is indeed entirely equal; in this world, the soul is entirely continuous;
in this world, the soul is purely immutable—O mind, why do you weep over that which is entirely equal? ||17||
Non-discrimination is non-awakening, and discrimination is non-awakening; likewise, non-conceptualization is non-awakening.
If there is indeed a single, uninterrupted awakening, then why do you weep, O mind, when all things are equal? 18.
There is indeed no state of liberation, nor a state of bondage; there is no state of merit, nor a state of sin.
There is no state of fullness, nor a state of emptiness. Why then do you weep, O Mānasi, when all is equal? 19.

If it is equal in being devoid of color and its absence, if it is equal in being devoid of cause and effect, and if it is equal in being devoid of difference and its absence—then why do you weep, O mind, when everything is equal? 20.

In this state where all thoughts are entirely uninterrupted, in this state where all thoughts are purely immobile, in this state where all thoughts are devoid of duality and the like—O mind, why do you weep, you who are equal toward all? (21)

O mind, why do you weep for that which is all-pervading, transcending all continuity, all-pervading and utterly stainless and immovable, all-pervading and devoid of day and night—[that which is] equal to everything? 22.
For there is no coming together of bondage and non-bondage, nor of union and separation;
nor is there any coming together of reasoning and discursive thought—why then do you weep, O Mānasi, when all things are equal? 23.
In this world, there is the rejection of both time and its opposite, and the rejection of even the slightest spark of fire.
Indeed, there is no rejection of absolute truth; why then do you weep, O mind, when all things are equal? 24.

O mind, why do you weep over that which is devoid of body and the state of being bodiless—indeed, that which is beyond dream and deep sleep, and supreme, transcending all designations and their application—as if it were something equal to everything else? 25.

Equal to the vast purity of the sky, equal in being entirely free from all [partiality], equal in having transcended essence, dispersion, and transformation—O mind, why do you weep, you who are equal to all? (26)

Here there is a greater detachment from dharma and adharma; here there is a greater detachment from the substantial and the insubstantial; here there is a greater detachment from desire and the absence of desire—why then do you weep, O mind, when all things are equal? (27)

Why do you weep, O Mānasi, for that which is entirely equal, devoid of pleasure and pain, free from sorrow and the absence of sorrow here, supreme, and beyond the distinction of teacher and disciple, being intent upon reality? (28)
It is said that there is no expansion or contraction of the sprout, nor any similarity or dissimilarity between the moving and the unmoving;
it is devoid of both non-investigation and investigation—why then do you weep, O mind, for that which is equal to all? 29.
Herein is stated the essence of the compendium of essences, namely, the distinction between one's own states of being.
Since the status of the senses as instruments toward objects is unreal, why do you weep, O mind, when everything is equal? 30.
The scriptures proclaim in many ways that this world, beginning with space, is like a mirage;
if it is entirely one, continuous, and equal to all, why then do you weep for that which is equal to everything? 31.
He finds, he finds—indeed, indeed not where there is the characteristic of desire; indeed, indeed not there.
Immersed in the flavor of equanimity, purified through meditation, the supreme ascetic utters the truth. 32.
Thus ends the fifth chapter. ||5||
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The scriptures proclaim in many ways that this world, beginning with space, is like a mirage;
yet if it is entirely one, continuous, and auspicious, then how can there be both the object of comparison and the comparison itself?
Indeed, [the Supreme] is devoid of case-endings and even the concept of case-grammar; it is truly beyond that which is produced or transformed.
If He is the one, uninterrupted, and entirely auspicious Śiva, then how can there be worship, and how can there be austerity? (2)
The mind alone is indeed continuous and all-pervading, for it is devoid of both the small and the great;
the mind alone is continuously and entirely auspicious—how could it be otherwise by means of thought or by means of speech? (3)

If the sun, the moon, and fire were all-pervasive, unitary, and continuous Śiva, how could there be the distinction between day and night, nor the refutation of that which is both risen and unrisen? (4)
"Free from the distinction between desire and the absence of desire" means free from the distinction between movement and non-movement.
And if all is eternally Śiva as one, without internal or external division, how can there be a mind that perceives such a distinction? ||5||
If it is devoid of essence and non-essence, and if it is devoid of emptiness and non-emptiness;
and if it is the first and the last, how can it be the one, the continuous, and the all-pervadingly auspicious? ||6||

If there is the negation of difference and division, if there is the negation of the knower and the known, and if there is the single, uninterrupted, all-pervading Śiva—then how can there be a third, and how can there be a fourth? (7)
"It is not true that what is spoken is unknown; nor is it true that what is known is unknown.
And if everything is eternally and entirely Śiva, how can there be objects, senses, intellects, and minds? (8)
The sky and the wind are not real; the earth and fire are not real.
If all is everywhere, without interval, and purely auspicious, then how can there be clouds, and how can there be water? (9)

If there is the refutation of an imagined world, and if there is the refutation of imagined deities, and if everything is one, continuous, and entirely auspicious, then how can there be any thought that discriminates between virtues and faults? 10.
For death and non-death are indeed a negation; for doing and not-doing are indeed a negation.
And if all is eternally one and auspicious, how can he speak of going and coming? 11.

Indeed, there is no difference between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), nor is there any distinction between cause and effect; yet if all is one, continuous, and entirely auspicious, how can you speak of both the person and the non-person? 12.
The third [state] is indeed not the meeting with suffering, nor is it the meeting with the qualities of the second;
for if everything were eternally and entirely auspicious, how could there be the old man, the youth, and the infant? (13)
Is it not the case that [the scripture] refers to that which is devoid of stages of life (āśrama) and castes (varṇa), and indeed refers to that which is devoid of causes and agents?
And if all is one, continuous, and auspicious, how can there be both the undestroyed and the destroyed, as well as the intellect? (14)
That which is swallowed and that which swallows are both unreal; that which is produced and that which is unproduced are both unreal.
And if [the world] were a single, continuous, entirely auspicious, and indestructible whole, how indeed could there be destruction? (15)

If there is a mind that finds no diversion in the diversionless, all-pervading, and eternal Śiva, then how could there be for it the notion that "the man has perished" or "the woman has perished"? 16.

If he is one who has transcended delusion and dejection, if he is one who has transcended doubt and sorrow, and if he has attained the singular, uninterrupted, and all-pervading auspiciousness where "I" and "mine" no longer exist—how then could there be [duality] again? (17)
Is it not the case that there is the destruction of merit and demerit? Is it not the case that there is the destruction of bondage and non-bondage?
And if all is eternally and universally auspicious, how can there be the experience of pleasure and pain, or even the thought of suffering? 18.
For there is no distinction between the sacrifice and the sacrificer, nor any distinction between the fire and its fuel;
and if you claim that all is one and undivided Śiva, how can there be fruits of action? 19.
Is he not indeed free from sorrow and joy? Is he not indeed free from pride and arrogance?
And if he is the absolute auspiciousness of all things in uninterrupted oneness, how then can there be the notions of passion and dispassion? 20.

For it is not a transformation caused by delusion or infatuation, nor is it a transformation caused by greed or desire; and if all is indeed eternally auspicious as one undivided whole, how then can there be the distinction between the intellect that lacks discernment and the intellect that possesses discernment? 21.
Indeed, "you" and "I" are never at any time a false consideration of lineage or birth;
since "I alone am Śiva, the ultimate reality," how could I offer salutations here? 22.
"Shattered by the deliberations of teacher and disciple," "shattered by the deliberations of instruction"—how can I here offer salutation, [thinking] "I myself am Śiva, the ultimate reality"? (23)
Since there is no division of imagined bodies, nor any division of imagined worlds, how can I here offer salutations, thinking "I myself am Śiva, the ultimate reality"? 24.
With passion, yet free from passion; never indeed [otherwise], but truly stainless, immovable, and pure—how can I offer salutation here, thinking "I myself am Śiva, the ultimate reality"? 25.
For the conceptual distinction between "embodied" and "disembodied" is neither a false practice nor is it the truth;
how then can I offer salutation here, thinking "I alone am Śiva, the ultimate reality"? ||26||
He finds it, he finds it—indeed, indeed, where there is no characteristic of desire; indeed, indeed, there [he finds it].
Immersed in the equality of flavors, purified through meditation, the supreme ascetic utters the truth. 27.
Thus ends the sixth chapter. ||6||
Now begins the seventh chapter.
With a necklace fashioned from the rags of the street, following a path devoid of both merit and demerit, he stands naked in an empty house, immersed in the pure, stainless state of equanimity. ||1||

How can one who is the object of perception yet devoid of being perceived or unperceived, whose skill is free from both the appropriate and inappropriate, and who is purified by the stainlessness of absolute reality, be considered a mere disputant in debate? (2)
Freed from the bonds of the fetters of desire, and devoid of conventional purity and conduct, thus tranquil and free from everything, they possess the reality that is pure and stainless. ||3||
How can there be here any consideration of the body or the disembodied? How can there be here any consideration of passion or dispassion?
Here, the reality itself is of the nature of the innate, having the form of the stainless and motionless sky. (4)
How does one find reality here, where there is both form and formlessness?
How can that supreme state, which has the nature of space, be made an object of perception here? (5)

The *haṃsa* is like the sky, uninterrupted; the *haṃsa* is the reality that is pure and stainless. How, then, can it here be divided or differentiated, being free from the transformations of bondage and its absence? (6)
Since everything is the uninterrupted reality alone, how can there be union or separation here?
Since everything is thus the supreme uninterruptedness, how can there be essence or non-essence here? (7)
The absolute reality is stainless, all-pervading, like the form of the sky, and eternally pure;
how then can there be attachment or detachment here? How can there be truth or falsehood here? (8)
The yogi is free from union and separation; the enjoyer is free from enjoyment and renunciation.
Thus he moves very slowly indeed, with a mind fixed upon the innate bliss that is imagined as such. 9.
How can one who is constantly joined with awakenings and non-awakenings, with duality and non-duality, be liberated here?
How can such a yogi be innate, stainless, pure, untainted, and an enjoyer of the state of equal flavor? 10.

Free from both the broken and the unbroken, yet appearing as the broken; free from both the ascendant and the non-ascendant, yet appearing as the ascendant—how, in this manner, is the essence of the world here, the reality of equal flavor, like the form of the sky? 11.

Constantly engaged in the relinquishing of everything, liberated by being free from all [conceptual] reality—how then can there be birth and death here, and how can there be action through meditations and concentrations? (12)
All this is a magical illusion, like a mirage in the desert;
Śiva alone exists, indivisible and formless. 13.
From the first dharma up to liberation, we are entirely devoid of effort;
how then do the wise imagine us through passion and dispassion? (14)
He finds it, he finds it—indeed, indeed, where there is no characteristic of desire; indeed, indeed, there [he finds it].
Immersed in the flavor of equanimity, purified through meditation, the supreme Avadhūta utters the truth. 15.
Thus ends the seventh chapter. ||7||
Now begins the eighth chapter.

By your procession, your omnipresence has been obscured; by your meditation, your transcendence of the mind has been obscured; by my praise, your transcendence of speech has been obscured. Forgive these three-fold offenses perpetually.

One whose intellect is unassailed by desires, self-controlled, gentle, pure, possessing nothing, free from longing, moderate in eating, tranquil, steadfast, and taking refuge in me—such a one is a sage (muni). ||2||
He is vigilant, profound in nature, steadfast, and has conquered the six internal enemies; he is free from pride yet bestows honor upon others, disciplined, friendly, compassionate, and wise.
Compassionate, free from malice toward all embodied beings, patient, rooted in truth, of irreproachable nature, impartial, and a benefactor to all. (4)

The characteristics of the Avadhūta should be known by the most excellent of Blessed Ones—those who know the true meaning of the letters of the Vedas and those who propound the Vedas and Vedānta. ||5||
Freed from the bonds of desire and stainless in the beginning, middle, and end, he dwells eternally in bliss; that is his characteristic, which is the letter A.
He by whom latent impressions (vāsanā) have been abandoned and who speaks that which is free from affliction—his characteristic is the letter 'Va', for he abides in the present. //7//

With limbs grey with dust, his mind shaken and free from disease, liberated from both meditative concentration and the power of retention—such is the characteristic of the one who utters the syllable "dhū. ||8||
He by whom the contemplation of reality has been maintained, who is devoid of the activities of thought, and who is liberated from darkness and egoism—“ta” is his defining characteristic. (9)
For those who read and listen to this work composed by Dattātreya Avadhūta, whose very nature is bliss, there is no further rebirth. 10.
Thus ends the eighth chapter. ||8||
Thus ends the Avadhūtagītā.
